extracted.intended_audience: general public; students and researchers of journalism and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the news media covering definitions, history, forms (print, broadcast, digital), journalistic genres and beats, production workflows, ethics and standards, news values, and contemporary challenges such as fake news and social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: News article components
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard components of a news article: Headline; Byline; Dateline; Report; Special report; Exclusive; Interview; Column; Editorial; Op-ed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements define the structure and presentation of news items; they are the building blocks of journalistic pieces and help signal authorship, timeliness, and genre to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Ws
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing style principle: the 'Five Ws' (who, what, when, where, why).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A basic journalistic guideline used to ensure essential facts are covered in news reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing style principle: the inverted pyramid structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most important information first, followed by supporting details and background; commonly used in news reporting to prioritize facts for readers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria that make events newsworthy, including concepts like 'above the fold' and 'man bites dog'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News values determine editorial selection and prominence of stories; see Harcup & O'Neill's revisiting of 'What is News?' for contemporary formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast story formats and lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Television/radio story formats: AVO, AVO Byte, Pkg, VO SOT, VOX POP, Ancho Visual. Example: AVO is short (30–40 seconds) with a script of three to four lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each broadcast format has conventions for parts (anchor, voice-over, sign-off), sequencing of visuals and speech, and target durations which shape scripting and editing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom production workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical process: reporters gather notes, photos/videos; organize material; determine the focus or 'peg'; write stories; stories are edited by news/copy editors or sub-editors; news desk decides headlines and may heavily rewrite; selected stories are laid out on dummy pages; chief editor approves content before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This workflow governs quality control, editorial judgment, assignment of bylines, and the final decision to publish; it also explains roles (reporter, editor, news desk, chief editor) and timing according to publication frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic beats (areas of coverage) such as Arts, Business, Data, Entertainment, Environment, Fashion, Local, Medicine, Music, Politics, Science, Sports, Technology, Traffic, Video games, War, Weather, World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats organize reporters' expertise and newsroom resources, shaping depth and consistency of coverage in topic areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres and formats of journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple journalistic genres including adversarial, advocacy, analytic, blogging, citizen, civic, collaborative, comics-based, community, database, enterprise, explanatory, feature story, gonzo, human-interest, immersion, infotainment/soft media, interpretive, investigative, long-form, narrative, New Journalism, opinion, peace, sensor, underground, visual, watchdog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different genres imply different goals, methods, ethical considerations, and expected standards of evidence and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking, copy editing, corrections, and spiking
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing functions that include copy editing, corrections, fact-checking, and spiking (withholding) material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices are essential parts of editorial standards to ensure accuracy, correct errors, and decide when material should not be published; they are listed under 'Editing' as quality-control mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes of ethics and journalism ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal and informal ethical standards and codes of ethics that govern journalistic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic ethics inform practices such as source handling, conflicts of interest, accuracy, independence, and transparency; the article lists 'Codes of ethics' and related topics (chequebook, churnalism) as ethical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and avoidance of false balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of objectivity in news coverage and the critique of media bias such as false balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity is a longstanding ideal in journalism; editors and reporters must be wary of 'false balance' where unequal positions are presented as equally credible without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media integrity (qualities of a trustworthy outlet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities that indicate media integrity: independence from private or political interests; transparency about financial interests; commitment to journalism ethics and standards; responsiveness to citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities are used to evaluate whether a media outlet serves the public interest and is resilient to institutional corruption, economy-of-influence, and political clientelism (concept devised for South East Europe but broadly applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence / Freedom of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence and legal guarantees such as freedom of the press and freedom of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal protections (e.g., First Amendment in U.S. history) and institutional safeguards support the press's ability to criticize government and operate independently; these are prerequisites for functioning journalism according to the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest standard for broadcasting licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Communications Act of 1934: (1) airways are public property; (2) commercial broadcasters are licensed to use the airways; (3) the main condition for use will be whether the broadcaster served 'the public interest, convenience, and necessity'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal standard historically constrained broadcast licensees and continues to be a benchmark for evaluating broadcasters' public-service obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsmagazine standard: in-depth context
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsmagazines (weekly) generally go more in-depth into stories than newspapers, trying to give readers an understanding of context rather than just the facts (example: TIME).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For longer-form periodic journalism, editorial emphasis shifts from immediacy to context, analysis, and authority-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online journalism and citizen publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Online (digital) journalism includes reporting produced or distributed via the Internet, by professional outlets and by citizens via blogs, vlogs, and social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Internet allows both formal and informal publication; this democratization increases variety but raises verification and reliability challenges (see 'Fake news').

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake news — definition and risk mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news: untruthful-on-purpose stories that purposely mislead the reader to think one way; proliferation increased with social media because anyone can share and rapidly spread information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights the difficulty of distinguishing fake from truthful articles online, the role of social media distribution in amplifying falsehoods, and the need for checking reliability and verifiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media consumption criteria and algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that make social-media-sourced news attractive: speed, novelty, format, variety, and a sense of community; algorithms deliver catered news and surface 'news influencers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These audience preferences and algorithmic curation affect what is produced and prioritized by outlets and influencers; the page cites Pew Research Center findings on usage and attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative journalism / muckraking
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism (muckrakers) exposes corrupt practices of officials and provides in-depth reporting that can influence policy; historically influential though sometimes criticized as sensationalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative work requires resources and often a progressive-era style of exposing wrongdoing; it is a quality dimension emphasizing depth, documentation, and public-impact reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source protection and reporter safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection of sources, defamation concerns, and safety of journalists are listed as challenges and legal/ethical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensuring sources' confidentiality and journalists' safety are part of ethical practice and legal considerations that affect how reporting is conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media plurality and editorial ownership concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about concentration of media ownership, media capture, and editorial independence are framed as challenges to healthy news ecosystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating outlets includes assessing ownership structures and the potential for economic or political influence to affect editorial content and diversity of viewpoints.
